sets.title: Central Bank Digital Currencies
sets.context:
Central bank digital currencies, or CBDCs, have moved from the realm of academic speculation to active experimentation in a remarkably short span. A CBDC is simply money issued directly by a country's central bank in digital form, distinct from the balances that commercial banks hold or the private cryptocurrencies that trade on exchanges. While the cash in your wallet is a direct claim on the central bank, the money in your bank account is a claim on a private lender; a retail CBDC would extend that direct, sovereign-backed claim into the digital world.

Proponents argue that a well-designed CBDC could lower the cost of payments, speed up settlement and extend financial services to millions who remain outside the formal banking system. Because it would be a public good rather than a profit-seeking product, a CBDC could in principle serve remote and low-income users whom private providers often neglect. For governments, it also promises faster and more transparent delivery of welfare payments, with less leakage along the way.

Yet the technology, still **nascent** in most economies, carries real risks. If citizens can hold money directly at the central bank, they may pull deposits out of commercial banks during moments of panic, draining the very institutions that fund loans to businesses and households. There are equally serious worries about privacy: a digital currency that records every transaction could hand the state an unprecedented window into private life. Poorly designed safeguards could **curtail** the financial freedoms that cash has long protected.

Most experts therefore counsel a cautious, deliberate approach. A two-tier model, in which the central bank issues the currency but private institutions manage customer-facing services, could preserve the role of banks while capturing the benefits of public digital money. Strong legal limits on data use, offline functionality and caps on individual holdings are among the guardrails being tested. Handled with care, a CBDC could modernise money for the digital age; handled carelessly, it could concentrate power and unsettle a financial system that depends, above all, on trust.
